title: The Travel Apps Worth Installing — and the Ones to Delete
metaDescription: A curated list of genuinely useful travel apps by category — maps, transport, translation, planning and safety — plus the ones not worth the storage.
excerpt: Most travel apps are a website with a worse interface. About a dozen genuinely earn their place on your phone.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
Search for travel apps and you will get lists of fifty. Almost all of them are a website wrapped in an icon, installed before one trip and deleted after it.

A useful phone for travel has maybe ten to fifteen apps that genuinely do something a browser cannot — usually because they work **offline**, integrate with your phone's hardware, or replace a physical object.

Here is the working set, by category, with the honest reason each one is there.

## Maps and Navigation

**A mainstream maps app with offline downloads.** The non-negotiable. Download the map area for every destination before you travel — this works without data, and it is the single most important pre-trip step for anyone visiting somewhere unfamiliar.

**A dedicated offline hiking and trails app.** Mainstream maps are weak on footpaths, trails and contour detail. For anything involving walking outside a city, a topographic app with downloadable regions is genuinely important — and in the mountains it is a safety item, not a convenience.

**A transit app for the specific city.** Major cities' own transport apps handle live times, disruptions and ticketing in ways general apps do not. Install on arrival, delete on departure.

## Transport and Flights

**One flight tracking app.** Push notifications for gate changes and delays, frequently faster than the airport boards and the airline itself. Worth having for this alone.

**Your airline's app**, for the trip. Mobile boarding passes, live rebooking during disruption, and — critically — the ability to rebook yourself during a mass delay while everyone else queues at a desk.

**A rail app for the region.** Europe's rail booking is fragmented across national operators, and a single aggregator app usually beats navigating five websites.

**Local ride-hailing.** Whichever service dominates locally, which is often not the global one. Install before you land, because signing up requires SMS verification that is easier on your home network.

![Technology travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1569697008488-e88ca8a71a39?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Accommodation and Planning

**One booking app**, not four. Pick a primary, use the browser for comparison.

**A collaborative trip planner**, if you travel with other people. This is the category with the largest gap between what most people use — a group chat and a spreadsheet — and what actually works. Group chats bury decisions under three hundred messages; spreadsheets get edited by one person and never opened by anyone else.

**Trypinn** exists for this specific problem: a shared itinerary the whole group can see and edit, route planning that shows whether the day's plan is physically possible, and expense tracking alongside it so nobody is reconstructing who paid for what at the end. If you only travel solo, a notes app is genuinely sufficient. If you travel in groups, the difference is substantial.

## Translation and Communication

**A translation app with offline language packs and camera translation.** Download the language pack before you go. Camera translation — pointing the phone at a menu or a sign — is the feature that does the most work in practice.

**A messaging app that locals actually use.** This varies by region, and the app everyone uses at home is frequently not the one used at your destination. Restaurants, guesthouses and drivers will often want to reach you on the local standard.

## Money

**Your bank's app**, with notifications on, so you see charges as they happen.

**A currency converter with offline rates.** Small, useful, and it stops you doing mental arithmetic badly at a market stall.

**An expense splitter for group trips** — or a planner that includes one, which avoids running two apps for one trip.

![Technology travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1505308144658-03c69861061a?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Documents and Storage

**A cloud storage app with offline files.** Scans of passports, visas, insurance, tickets and vaccination records, downloaded for offline access. This is the app you will be most grateful for on the one bad day.

**A password manager.** Essential if you are logging into anything on unfamiliar networks, and the only sane way to have different passwords for the six accounts you create while travelling.

**A note-taking app**, for confirmation numbers, addresses in the local script, and the name of the restaurant someone recommended.

## Safety

**An offline first aid reference.**

**Your country's travel advisory app**, if it has one — several governments offer registration for citizens abroad, which matters in a genuine emergency.

**A VPN**, for using public Wi-Fi in cafés, airports and hotels. Any network you do not control is a network you should not bank on unprotected.

**A local emergency number reference.** They are not 911 or 112 everywhere, and you will not want to look it up when you need it.

## Genuinely Situational

- **A star chart app** for dark sky destinations
- **A dive log** for diving trips
- **A currency-specific tipping guide** if you are somewhere with unfamiliar norms
- **An eSIM provider's app**, if your data plan is managed in one

## What to Delete

**Single-destination city guide apps.** A guidebook with a worse interface and no updates. Download an offline map and read a real guide.

**Most itinerary-scraping apps.** They parse your email to build a timeline, which duplicates what your calendar and your booking confirmations already do, in exchange for reading your inbox.

**Apps for services you will use once.** The tour operator's app, the museum's app, the hotel chain's app for a single stay. Book through a browser.

**Multiple booking apps.** Comparison happens in a browser. You need one app for managing the booking you made.

**Anything demanding permissions it has no reason to want.** A currency converter asking for your contacts is telling you something about its business model.

## The Pre-Trip Phone Routine

Twenty minutes the night before, which prevents most of the problems people have with phones abroad:

1. **Download offline maps** for every destination
2. **Download offline translation packs**
3. **Save documents offline** in cloud storage — do not rely on streaming them
4. **Screenshot everything critical** into one album: boarding passes, booking confirmations, visa approvals, insurance details, the first night's address
5. **Set up your eSIM** or check roaming
6. **Charge the power bank.** An uncharged power bank is a heavy paperweight
7. **Turn off automatic photo backup over cellular**, unless you want to watch your data allowance vanish
8. **Share your itinerary** with someone not travelling with you

That last one costs nothing and is the single most useful safety measure available to a solo traveller. Someone who knows roughly where you are meant to be today is worth more than any app on this list.
